item.title: Trump's 'pocket rescission' could cancel $810 million before Congress can act
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. President Donald Trump goes to speak to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 26, 2026. —Samuel Corum—Sipa/Bloomberg via Getty Images President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is seeking to cancel almost $1 billion in federal funding, sidestepping congressional approval and earning criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. Using a controversial move known as a “pocket rescission,” Trump said he wanted to nullify $810 million in spending that Congress had approved for programs and agencies, much of which would serve immigrants, minorities, and children. Read More: A Debt Ceiling Fight Looms in 2027. Could a Democratic Congress Make it the Last One? Over half of the cuts would land on the Health and Human Services (HHS) Department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, according to a request sent to House Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday. It said that rescinding the funds is “consistent with the Administration's goal of ending the use of Federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens, putting Americans first.” In a statement accompanying the request, the Trump Administration also called the funds “wasteful” and “harmful.” The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog, has asserted, however, that the move is an illegal sidestepping of the constitutionally protected separation of powers—chiefly, Congress's power of the purse. What is a pocket rescission? A “pocket rescission” is not a formal or legal term; it was coined to reference a “ pocket veto ,” a process in which a bill fails to become law because the President does not sign it within 10 days and Congress’s adjournment prevents its return. Similarly, the “pocket rescission” aims to withdraw allocated funding without direct congressional intervention. The timing is important when it comes to pocket rescissions. In order to be fully effective, this “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO). The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), helmed by Director Russell Vought, submitted the requests Friday and holds that the move is valid under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act (ICA). The Impoundment Control Act was created in response to President Richard Nixon’s heavy use of impoundments to achieve his policy goals. It has since been used to limit or regulate a president’s ability to control spending that has already been appropriated by building in 45 days of continuous congressional session. During this time, Congress is meant to review a President’s rescission requests and either approve them or see the funds released as planned. Trump’s request to cancel $810 million in funding, however, came just five days before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, all but ensuring that Congress will not have time to review the proposal in full or prevent the cuts from going into effect. It is not the first time Trump has used this strategy to thwart spending attempts. He submitted a request on Aug. 28, 2025, to cancel $4.9 billion in foreign aid funds approved by Congress, including $3.2 billion that had been allocated to USAID . Although the move was contested, the Supreme Court last year stayed a lower court injunction requiring roughly $4 billion covered by the rescission request to be obligated. The GAO claims that the move is illegal, writing on its website that this application of the ICA would “cede Congress’s power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds.” “If Congress wanted a president to have that authority, it would need to change the law,” it continues. Zachary Price, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, says that the move is an “abuse” of the ICA. “It’s perverse to read that as, instead, creating this mechanism for unilaterally canceling funds,” Price tells TIME, adding that this interpretation is not supported by a lot of “historical practice.” The maneuver seeks to withhold the funds until they expire at the end of the fiscal year, leaving Congress little time to respond. In this case, Price says, it further showcases how the ICA is being manipulated. The government “shouldn't have a lot of money left over at the end of the fiscal year if you've been spending it as you go in the way the statute contemplates,” he says. He also points out that the American government is distinctly separated into three branches, with Congress, sitting in the legislative branch, being given the power to pass legislation—or, in this case, cancel funds that have already been appropriated. It has been explicitly separated from the authority of the executive branch and the President. Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, says it even plainer than Price: “The administration has picked a bunch of things that they hate, and they say, ‘Well, we're just not going to do those.’” The Supreme Court’s intervention last year did not constitute a ruling on the authority of pocket rescissions, meaning that the Trump Administration's latest use of the tactic could face new legal challenges. Which federal programs would lose funding and what’s at stake? The largest portion of this year’s proposed cuts will target HHS programs providing nonprofit services for refugees and unaccompanied minors. Trump’s request would withdraw $567 million from those services. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was also impacted, with a request to cancel funding for nonprofits that provide mental health services and social services to migrants. Another cut targets almost $25 million that had been slated for the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students. The Housing and Urban Development Department’s housing counseling services are also named amid the rescissions; the Trump Administration said that the program included non-governmental organizations with “divisive and DEI-centric agendas.” The Trump Administration also aims to cancel $15 million from a Department of Justice office that focuses on reducing racial tensions, in addition to $10 million that had been allocated to the Minority Business Development Agency, which supports minority entrepreneurs. “I assume that they're picking money to cancel based on some political calculus about what they can get away with,” Price says. When looking at the bigger picture, he argues this is just one maneuver in several to “establish stronger executive control over spending.” The move also risks future negotiations in Congress, Price says. He explains that this application of the ICA would make it harder for Democrats and Republicans to compromise over spending if they anticipate that the sitting President will simply swoop in and cancel funding after thoughtful agreements have been reached. “If the executive branch can come in and effectively impose a more kind of party line view of the spending, then you know why would people agree to the package in the first place?” he asks. Can Congress stop Trump’s pocket rescission? The rescission has earned blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who believe that the move sidesteps Congress's authority. Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, lambasted the move on social media Friday evening , saying she would “work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.” “This move shows that OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.” Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, Collins’s Democratic counterpart on the Appropriations Committee, called the move “theft from the American people.” “Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because Vought is saying their votes don’t count,” Murray said in a statement on X. The August 2025 pocket rescission was challenged in an existing lawsuit brought by nonprofits, including AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, over the Administration’s prior foreign aid freeze. In September, the Supreme Court allowed the funds covered by the rescission request to remain withheld while litigation continued. This year, similar lawsuits are likely to emerge—but how they might shape future ICA actions remains to be seen. According to Kogan, this move sets up a potential battle in Congress to claw back these funds in the next fiscal cycle by reappropriating funds to the same programs. “One thing that Congress could do is they could say ‘I know you illegally didn't spend it this year, but take that money we’re going to slap it right back on,’” he says. “That doesn't make [Vought] spend it next year, but it does say that we are going to make sure this money gets out the door, even if it's years late.” This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/09/26/what-is-a-pocket-rescission-inside-trump-s-move-to-cancel-810-million-in-federal-funding/

item.title: Ex-CIA officer's novel alleges grave dysfunction in deep-cover operations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A new, previously suppressed book by a former CIA officer paints a satirical and slashing portrait of the agency’s deep-cover spying program as riven by systematic dysfunction. The book, “The Pickle Factory,” written by an ex-CIA nonofficial cover officer, under the pen name Sam R. Oyken, is billed as a work of fiction. Though often fantastical, it contains thinly veiled true-life details about the inner workings of the agency’s spying operations, according to former CIA officials. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Most CIA officers work under what’s known as “official cover” and generally masquerade as U.S. diplomats abroad. NOCs, who often pose as businessmen or consultants, have no overt connections to the U.S. government and therefore operate without diplomatic immunity. Because of the potential dangers of their missions and the clandestine participation of American companies who provide cover to these officers, NOCs’ operations are closely guarded inside the CIA. “The Pickle Factory,” published in late July, is the culmination of what the author characterized as a multiyear battle against agency censors, who first rejected publication of the manuscript in 2014. The Washington Post is referring to him by his pen name, as the former NOC remains undercover. Former CIA employees are required to submit all work potentially relevant to their agency careers to the CIA’s Prepublication Classification Review Board for potential redaction, to expunge it of allegedly classified information. “They insisted for years after I submitted the manuscript of my novel that I couldn’t publish a single word, a straight-up First Amendment violation,” said Oyken in an interview. Then-CIA Executive Director Meroe Park reversed the blanket ban in 2017, but the agency then “tried to redact more than half of the book, which I fought, redaction by redaction, until they folded,” he said. Park did not return a request for comment. A spokesperson for the CIA declined to comment. The saga surrounding the book first trickled into public view in 2015, when Oyken - then using the alias Mack Charles in court documents - lodged a $25 million complaint against the CIA in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging that agency officials conspired to fire the 13-year CIA veteran because they disapproved of his romantic relationship with another deep-cover officer to whom he was engaged and who was two decades younger. Oyken was fired from the CIA in December 2010 and accused the agency of suppressing his book as part of a broader retaliation campaign, according to the 2015 lawsuit. His suit against the agency was dismissed on procedural grounds in March 2016. The passage of time, and changes in agency leadership, appear to have attenuated concerns surrounding the book, and the CIA gave Oyken final approval to publish “The Pickle Factory” in early 2026. Books by former NOCs have often met fierce resistance inside the CIA. The 2019 publication of “Life Undercover ,” a memoir by former deep-cover officer Amaryllis Fox Kennedy, became embroiled in controversy when reports emerged that she did not receive final CIA approval to publish her book. Fox Kennedy - who served until recently as a senior official within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Office of Management and Budget inside the Trump administration - did not appear to face sanction by the agency. The CIA did sue another ex-NOC, writing under the pen name Ishmael Jones, for publishing a critical 2008 nonfiction account of his own experience inside the deep-cover program. Jones’s book, “The Human Factor ,” had not been reviewed by agency censors. In 2012, a federal judge ordered Jones to forfeit any profit from future sales of the book. “The Pickle Factory” dredges up what many CIA alumni consider an unhappy chapter in the history of the agency’s deep-cover program . In addition to skewering a number of former senior agency officials who oversaw the NOC cadre - whose biographies (and, at times, names) are only lightly fictionalized - the book recounts the agency’s post-9/11 push to procure, and perhaps surreptitiously redirect for other purposes, billions of dollars in funding earmarked by Congress for a vastly expanded NOC program. The post-9/11 NOC expansion was a real-life “debacle,” said a former deep-cover colleague of Oyken’s, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly address sensitive intelligence operations, “where results were secondary, receipts were primary, and spending was king.” Much of Oyken’s work with the agency remains shrouded in secrecy. His career bridged two eras at CIA, according to the same former colleague: the bespoke, targeted deep-cover program extant at CIA before Sept. 11, 2001, and the engorged NOC program that followed it, with younger, poorly trained NOCs being rushed into the field. One part of this initiative involved deploying groups of these new NOCs to roughly a dozen secret “platforms” abroad; by 2008, almost all these efforts had folded in failure. Oyken joined the CIA in 1996 as a French-speaking graduate of Harvard Law School who worked for the white-shoe law firm Covington & Burling before joining the agency, according to a declassified tranche of documents reviewed by The Post. In 1999, he was selected for a 20-year deep-cover assignment abroad, an unusually long posting for NOC officers. The documents, some of which were redacted, point to a posting somewhere in Europe. That assignment was cut short for reasons unclear in the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. The mission ended because of a counterintelligence issue unrelated to Oyken’s performance, according to another former CIA official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe clandestine operations. Oyken was subsequently assigned to be an instructor to CIA trainees, according to the documents. He was then selected for a managerial role inside the NOC program, according to court documents as well as the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. Oyken is identified in the declassified papers as a “QRN,” which former CIA colleagues say refers to “Quick Reaction NOC,” an elite group of deep-cover officers who often travel on non-U.S. passports to undertake highly sensitive intelligence-gathering or eavesdropping-related missions abroad. The court documents suggest that, after his stint as a trainer, Oyken served as QRN chief, stating that he “exercised supervisory authority over more than 80 subordinates, including other NOC Operations Officers in his Group.” Oyken’s dismissal from the CIA was a contentious and bitter affair, per both sets of documents. His overseers accused him of financial improprieties, inappropriate romantic relationships with subordinates, absenteeism in his managerial duties and bullying of underlings. Agency officials also lamented his lack of recruitments, according to the declassified tranche. His was “a chronic case of long-term behavior that has completely eroded the confidence management has in this officer,” said one declassified agency memorandum reviewed by The Post. Oyken strenuously contested the allegations. “They came at me like a pack of wild dogs,” he said in an interview. The declassified documents reveal an aggressive investigation into Oyken, including his finances. In one partially redacted 2009 email, an incoming NOC program chief decries the “loose approach” to deep-cover deployments, vowing that Oyken “will be coming home the first day I’m in the chair.” He was “the kind of china I’m looking forward to breaking” upon taking over the program, writes the soon-to-be NOC boss. Oyken characterizes the deep-cover program as hidebound and in acute need of reform. “There’s a certain kind of CIA manager who prefers that NOCs be full-time accountants rather than spies out taking risks,” he said. “Meanwhile they themselves squander billions of dollars and turn a blind eye while their cronies make off with stacks of gold bars.” In May 2026, David J. Rush, a senior CIA official working on ultrasecret intelligence-gathering programs, was arrested on charges of stealing public funds, including the alleged theft of $40 million worth of gold bars from the agency. Though formally a work of fiction, “The Pickle Factory” clearly puts the real-world CIA in its crosshairs. “It’s almost impossible for outsiders to grasp how mediocre the agency has become,” Oyken said. “Only a novel-length treatment could do the topic justice.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/ex-cia-officer-novel-alleges-162408657.html

item.title: Sen. John Fetterman says it's 'entirely possible' Democrats take back Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania said Saturday that it's "entirely possible" his party could win control of the Senate in the midterm elections, but he also left the door open on his own political future. "Let's revisit after the midterm," Fetterman told CBS News' Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin . Democrats faced an uphill battle heading into the midterm cycle as they sought control the upper chamber, with 53 Republicans currently in the Senate and a map that appeared more favorable to the GOP. But as affordability issues have persisted in the Trump administration and amid the unpopular war with Iran, the picture has appeared to improve for Democrats as they aim to secure a majority in the Senate. Fetterman, who delivered Democrats a crucial victory in a closely watched race in 2022, has been under scrutiny in recent years for breaking with his party, spurring questions about his future. Asked whether he would leave the Democratic Party, Fetterman said Saturday that he doesn't "have a reason to." And he emphasized, "I am not a Republican." But he cautioned that people should wait until the midterm elections to "see what I do." "Let's see what happens if I happen to be 51 — I don't know," Fetterman said. Fetterman shocked many Democrats when he made a video appearance at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month introducing his counterpart, GOP Sen. Dave McCormick, while vowing to work with President Trump on steel. But Fetterman said Saturday, "I have no path as a Republican." The Pennsylvania Democrat said, "There are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community, that does not exist in the Republican Party." "How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So wait until after the midterm and see what happens," he said. "And now, if we do win and I'm 51, people can remember, 'hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania." Pennsylvania is one of only two states in the country represented by one Democrat and one Republican in the Senate, alongside Wisconsin. A third state, Maine, has one Republican senator and one independent who caucuses with Democrat. Pennsylvania has flipped between supporting Democrats and Republican presidents in recent elections. On whether he'll seek reelection in 2028 , Fetterman said he's been actively fundraising, but he also indicated that the decision will come after the midterms. Fetterman posed the question, "Where's the Democratic Party at right now?" He pointed to attendance at a nearby event with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and "the energy" among the party, which has seen a series of wins by insurgent Democrats in recent months. He cited his commitment to Israel as an issue underscoring his divergence from some of the party, adding, "more and more members of my caucus are becoming more and more anti-Israel." He also pointed to the recent government shutdowns as an issue he diverged from the bulk of Democrats on, arguing that he's "putting the country over the party" and fighting for workers. "Do you think it's right and smart to shut our government down? No, Democrats, we used to say, 'No, never, never do that,'" Fetterman said. "And that put me at the odds of my caucus, saying, 'It's wrong.'" Fetterman said he's "chosen to be country over the party, knowing that some of these decisions are going to put me at odds." Asked whether he expects Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to remain leader if Democrats take the majority, and whether he would vote for him, Fetterman said, "Yes, I mean, there's no one making a move." Fetterman called a Marist poll that shows Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek up eight points in Iowa "shocking," among other races where Democrats are leading in some polls. He pointed to Schumer's recruiting efforts, saying, "If people are angry at Chuck Schumer, it's undeniable, he has recruited an incredibly strong class." "I don't sharpen blades for Chuck Schumer, and there might be some people there that refuse to say it, but it's not helpful to go after our leader because we have no idea until we wait until the midterm," Fetterman said. "It's irrelevant until what happens in the midterm." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/john-fetterman-democrats-senate-midterm-plans/

item.title: Trump says U.S.-Iran talks will continue this week despite rejecting latest offer
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. and Iranian officials said Sunday they still see a chance of a negotiated solution to the Iran war despite President Donald Trump's rejection of Tehran's latest offer. Trump told Axios on Sunday that he expected U.S. negotiators to continue indirect talks with Iran this week. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But hostile rhetoric on both sides underscored the difficulty of any diplomatic efforts. "We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. … We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC News on Sunday. At the same time, he said, "we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose." "If they are serious that they want a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, now there is the possibility," Araghchi said. On Saturday, Trump said he had rejected Iran's latest proposal to end the war. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters. But Axios reported that Trump had confirmed during a Sunday phone interview that there were plans for indirect talks. "I expect more talks with Iran [this week]. They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand," Trump said, according to Axios. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told NBC News's "Meet the Press" that the recent Iranian proposal was a "cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable." The proposal included demands that the United States lift sanctions on Iran, release frozen assets and end the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports, he said. "At the end of the day, of course, this has to end in some type of arrangement. But he's going to leave all options on the table to get there," Waltz told NBC News. Araghchi had said Tehran's offer was similar to the memorandum of understanding both sides reached in June. Both Araghchi and Waltz accused the other's country of engaging in negotiations only to violate their terms. "Again they offered negotiation, again we accepted, and again they attacked us in the middle of negotiations. … But I am still trying diplomacy because I think we shouldn't miss any chance for peace," Araghchi said. Waltz told NBC News it was "common sense" that the president did not have much confidence in Iran's offer after the country violated the memorandum of understanding brokered in June. Negotiations between Iran and the U.S., both directly and indirectly, to end the war have been on and off since a few weeks after it began on Feb. 28. In June, both countries reached an initial truce, signing a memorandum of understanding that included a two-month timeline to hammer out terms for lasting peace, including tackling differences over Iran's nuclear program, sanctions and control over the Strait of Hormuz. The ceasefire quickly unraveled, and the 60-day deadline passed last month with no breakthroughs. Iranian officials pursued a flurry of diplomatic meetings in New York last week during the U.N. General Assembly. Trump administration officials held talks with the Iranian delegation through mediators, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said in an X post. Trump had told the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday that Iran could make a deal to end the war or face "annihilation." The Iranian delegation walked out of the chamber. The following day, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the U.N. that Iran was "ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force." Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-says-u-iran-slated-173419570.html

item.title: Attorney General Blanche says White House press access is a privilege, not a right
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday addressed the Trump administration's decision to ban three mainstream news outlets from accessing the White House, saying that President Donald Trump had not "denied access" to the organizations and asserting that it is a "privilege ... not a right" to be at the White House. "The president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it. This is -- what the president has said is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news," Blanche said in an exclusive interview with "This Week" co-anchor Martha Raddatz. "There's still obviously litigation going on, but the important thing, Martha, is to know that ... being in the White House is a privilege. It's not a right." In the early hours Thursday, Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order that required the White House to temporarily restore credentials of journalists working for CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Kelly said in his ruling that he believed the outlets cleared the "high bar" required to grant a TRO. ABC News - U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche on ABC's "This Week." Journalists were allowed back onto the White House grounds later Thursday and primary television pool coverage resumed Friday for the final day of Chinese President Xi Jinping's official state visit. But on Saturday, there was no TV pool coverage for the president's trip to a football game in Tennessee; CNN was scheduled to be network covering the president that day, but they said their access to Air Force One was blocked. Blanche said it wasn't unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed onto the president's plane. "The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One. This wasn't a a one-time denial of CNN. There's all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying," according to Blanche, who added, "it's not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it's common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president." Judge concludes Trump's White House media ban hearing with no ruling Blanche claimed the three news outlets that were subject to the White House ban "refuse to report anything accurately," which he said presented a "national security problem." "When you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House that affects our relationship with our foreign partners, that affects our relationship with our foreign enemies -- and so this is just not about the fact that they're refusing to report accurate news. It's all about the information that the American people have a right to hear coming out of of our what should be respected media outlets." Judge Kelly, however, was skeptical in his TRO ruling that national security was the true reason for the ban. "For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House -- instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting," Kelly wrote. Hours after announcing the ban on social media, Trump was asked in the Oval Office if there was any "particular reason or particular story" that prompted it. "No, no. It's -- it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it," the president said. On "This Week," Blanche said he wouldn't "get into what the judge says" because the litigation is ongoing, but added "our position has been clear from the beginning. What they say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security." When Raddatz pressed Blanche to provide specific examples of stories with which the White House has taken issue, Blanche declined to do so. Artificial intelligence 'vital to our national security' On the issue of artificial intelligence, the attorney general echoed the president's position on the technology, describing it as "so important and vital to our national security interests and to the success of this country that the United States lead in this space." Trump has said it's critical that the U.S. continues to dominate the AI space, citing competition with China specifically. Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Shutterstock - PHOTO: President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping depart the National Archives Museum in Washington, September 25, 2026. "Whoever wins AI, WINS! We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I’m going to keep it that way! I’m not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself," he posted on social media Monday. Some AI company leaders are calling for an industry-wide slowdown amid growing concerns about how the rapid pace of development. Multiple incidents of AI agents acting autonomously have come to light in recent months, including instances where AI agents infiltrated outside companies without the agents' parent companies' awareness as it happened. 23 states urge Congress to regulate AI, warn of risks to national security and infrastructure Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that OpenAI agent "infiltrated" a government public health website earlier this summer. This weekend, OpenAI confirmed that its models interacted with U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, behavior the company discovered amid an ongoing review into its AI agents' behaviors. Blanche acknowledged that "there's going to be adjustments that have to be made" around AI as the industry continues to develop, but he argued the companies themselves already have the ability to "adjust the technology" as needed. "In the meantime, the answer is not to just try to all of a sudden try to regulate this in a way that will make us second or third place in the world as far as being being the leaders in this space," Blanche said. During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, Trump said of AI, "We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice." Asked what that meant, Blanche said, "What it means is that we have a ton of laws -- criminal laws, civil laws -- that are already in place and on the books that allow us to charge individuals, to charge companies in the right circumstances when there's crimes committed, and so the answer isn't always more laws, more laws, more laws." "When there are crimes committed, we have a lot of tools already, and the federal Title 18 gives us a lot of a lot of ways to go after criminals and bad actors in the AI space and other spaces," Blanche continued. "So when the president talks about about the fact that the Department of Justice and the FBI and [Homeland Security Investigations], they can go and arrest bad actors in this space, that's what he means, and it's true, and that's what we're doing." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/ag-blanche-addresses-white-house-news-outlet-ban/story?id=136794733

item.title: Waltz says Iran wanted sanctions relief first. Tehran says that's not the full story.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said Sunday that President Donald Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal because Tehran wanted sanctions relief and access to "billions in frozen assets" before negotiating an end to its nuclear program. "They were asking for everything up front, with a promise that they would then talk," Waltz said on CNN's "State of the Union" when asked what Trump objected to. In a separate interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Waltz called the proposal "a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable." He said the U.S. would ultimately need to reach "some type of agreement" with Iran, but Trump would keep all options on the table. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in an interview later on the same NBC program, pushed back on Waltz's account and told host Kristen Welker that Iran was prepared to open the strait if the U.S. met its conditions, including releasing frozen assets and allowing Iranian oil sales. "I am surprised that the ambassador is talking about a seven-day plan, as he has not read it," Araghchi said. "Maybe he has not been given a copy." On Saturday, Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for the U.S. lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales and committing to a seven-day ceasefire that would include Lebanon. In an interview with CBS's "Face the Nation" recorded Friday and aired Sunday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian described the proposal as a staged approach based on an earlier U.S.-Iran agreement. "Ultimately, the requests that were included in that memorandum and MOU have now been broken down into stages so that we can proceed according to those stages," Pezeshkian said. "These are things that both sides need to open up first, then we can sit down at the negotiating table and discuss other issues at hand." "They wanna make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters. "We're winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait." The Wall Street Journal reported Friday , citing U.S. officials, that Trump has told aides he expected to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms. Asked about the report, Waltz said, "I don't think that the president has said that himself; that's some reporting by a newspaper." "What the president has said and said here at his U.N. speech was that the Iranians are miscalculating that he's taking into account politics here," Waltz added. On "Meet the Press," Waltz also declined to confirm the reported timetable, saying Trump would "leave all options on the table." Araghchi, asked about the same report, said Iran was "fully prepared for the war to be resumed" but remained open to diplomacy. "It is up to President Trump to choose," he said. This comes as the war in Iran and rising gas prices put pressure on Republicans ahead of the November midterms. item.title: Pope Leo visits Lourdes and criticizes legalization of assisted dying as 'false compassion'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Pope Leo XIV criticized the legalization of medically assisted dying , calling it immoral and an example of "false compassion" during a visit on Sunday to Lourdes, the Catholic shrine in France associated with miraculous cures of the sick. "It is precisely in the name of this inalienable dignity of the human person that we must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," said Leo, prompting applause from the crowd gathered to see him. "What is legal is not necessarily moral." On his third day in France, Leo again waded into the end-of-life debate that has erupted in countries around the world. It roiled French politics for years before resulting recently in legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. Leo's visit to the once staunchly Catholic and officially secular France has been marked by huge crowds — 800,000 at Leo's Mass on Paris' iconic Place de la Concorde — and his messaging against abortion and assisted dying. Many who attended the pope's Mass on Sunday were in wheelchairs, and he later visited a care center for sick people on Lourdes' grounds. He sought to encourage those who live in "terrible pain" that they have inherent dignity that no law or algorithm can "eliminate." Lourdes became a major pilgrimage destination after the Catholic Church officially recognized visions of the Virgin Mary reported here by a young girl in 1858. The site near the Spanish border draws millions of pilgrims each year, especially sick and disabled believers hoping for a cure from the famed spring water in the Lourdes grotto where the visions purportedly occurred. Since arriving in France, Leo has repeatedly called for a renewed respect for life in keeping with Catholic teaching that all human life must be protected and defended from conception until natural death. The teaching translates into firm opposition to abortion, euthanasia and medically assisted dying. In Lourdes, where the church has recognized 72 "miraculous" cures as authentic, the question of respecting even the most frail, sick and vulnerable is particularly acute. "Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said in his homily. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God." Leo meets with clergy abuse survivors More recently, Lourdes has also become a place of healing for survivors of clergy sexual abuse. Leo met with seven survivors on Sunday, including one who was abused as an adult, in recognition of the new frontier of the abuse crisis facing the church. Survivors described the pope as sincere despite some differences of opinion following the two-hour meeting. "There was something sincere with him. Every word was chosen; every word had a meaning. There were many emotions," Jérôme Guillement said. Guillement told a local French TV station that they talked about abuse prevention at all levels. "There are different opinions, but from his point of view, there is a systemic dimension that still exists," he said. Olivier Mardi said the pope understands that he must work with victims. "He reacted well to our very concrete proposals ... He said that we must reopen hope, and it takes seriousness to seize it," Mardi told France's LCI news channel. The French church has endured a brutal reckoning with its legacy of abuse. An independent report in 2021 estimated 330,000 children had been abused over 70 years by some 3,000 priests and church workers. Despite criticism of the report's methodology and conclusions, French bishops put in place an independent system of compensation for victims that to date has recommended the church pay out more than 20 million euros, or $22.7 million. During a meeting with French bishops on Sunday morning, Leo praised their response to victims and urged them to continue. But he also acknowledged that the cratering in priestly vocations in the French church is related to the scandal, given the priesthood is now sometimes viewed with suspicion. "For priestly vocations to flourish, the priest must be welcomed, accepted, and loved," Leo said. On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of victims wrote an open letter asking him to acknowledge the church's responsibility in the scandal, highlighting what critics see as the conflict of interest of bishops being asked to be both spiritual fathers to their priests and judges when they abuse. "The Church must relinquish its position as both judge and party to the proceedings," the victims wrote in the letter published by French newspaper Liberation. The victims also complained that only seven of them would meet with Leo, chosen by the church. Monsignor Pierre-Antoine Bozo, spokesperson for the bishops' conference, said Leo intentionally wanted to keep the group small to facilitate an intimate encounter. "When it comes to listening to them, you can't have 50 people in front of you," he said. "So I think that's really what the pope chose: to listen so that we can act and respond more effectively." In Lourdes, Leo was also reminded of a prickly abuse case inherited from Pope Francis. The façade of one of the Lourdes basilicas was designed by the Rev. Marko Rupnik, a religious mosaic artist. Rupnik is currently on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them starting in the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. His case was covered up for three decades by his Jesuit superiors, and even Francis was suspected of having protected his fellow Jesuit. In response to a media outcry, Francis ordered a canonical trial in 2024, which is ongoing. In a letter to Leo ahead of his trip, five women who say they were abused by Rupnik praised Micas' decision to cover the mosaics. But they criticized the Vatican's handling of their case and the three decades it has taken for them to be heard. "This prolonged and loud silence has been experienced by us, the victims, as a further, continuous violence," they wrote. TAIPEI, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The United States "very much" understands Taiwan's defence needs and the severe military threat it faces from China, a senior ‌Taiwanese diplomat said on Sunday, following a Washington summit between the US ‌and Chinese leaders. Democratically governed Taiwan, which China claims as its own territory, has been waiting for months ​for US President Donald Trump to approve a new arms sales package worth some $14 billion, following up on a record $11 billion deal unveiled last December. After meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in May, Trump said he was keeping the latest arms ‌sales package in abeyance. Trump ⁠has not mentioned the sale since last week's summit, saying only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan. Speaking to ⁠reporters in Taipei, Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi pointed to comments by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that military sales to anyone require the same careful consideration. "Taiwan ​faces a ​severe situation in the Taiwan Strait. Even ​though China's economy is declining, ‌it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under this context, the US very much understands our defence needs," he said. Washington also understands Taiwan's determination to invest in its military, Chen added. "We do continuously communicate with them, and we believe the US understands the situation we face and our determination on defence investment completely." The ‌United States is bound by law to provide ​Taiwan with the means to defend itself. China ​has repeatedly called for military ​sales to end. David Perdue, the US ambassador to China, told CNBC ‌on Friday that there has been ​no change in Taiwan ​policy by Trump, including on arms sales. Chen said Taiwan had received confirmation "from our American friends repeatedly that US policy toward Taiwan remains unchanged". Taiwan's government ​rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying ‌only the island's people can decide their future. China has rebuffed repeated calls ​for talks by Taiwan President Lai Ching-te, whom it calls a "separatist". item.title: Christa Pike could be the 1st woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date [Tennesse Department of Corrections] Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee. Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says. Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest. Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull. A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men. Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting". Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder [Family handout] But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped. Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence. In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider. "It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence. "Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness." Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parents [Christa Pike] In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened. But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge. In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since. Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her. "Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says. Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation." Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable." Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say [Christa Pike] 'She should pay for it' Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution. A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy. Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021 . Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before. The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps. On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it. Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution. "She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments. Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did." May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006 [J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via Reuters] "My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added. "There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting." The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution. The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want. "We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed." Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption. "When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says. "These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else." Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime. "People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says. "Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live." Three men will be executed on the same day as death penalties rise in US Lisa Montgomery: Looking for answers in the life of a killer Biden commutes most federal death sentences This article originally appeared on BBC at https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c6pwl9g9ne1lo?xtor=AL-72-%5Bpartner%5D-%5Byahoo.north.america%5D-%5Bheadline%5D-%5Bnews%5D-%5Bbizdev%5D-%5Bisapi%5D

item.title: FBI ousts 2 agents who investigated alleged harassing calls to Stephen Miller's wife
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, and his wife, Katie Miller, attend the White House Easter Egg Roll on Monday, April 21, 2025. - Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call/Sipa USA Two veteran FBI agents overseeing counterterrorism operations in the nation’s capital have been removed from their jobs and reassigned over the handling of an investigation involving Katie Miller, the conservative podcaster and wife of senior White House adviser Stephen Miller, according to two people familiar with the move. Michael Burgwald, the special agent in charge of counterterrorism matters at the FBI’s Washington Field Office, and his deputy, Courtland Rae, were ousted from their positions by bureau leadership after investigators determined that allegedly harassing phone calls Katie Miller received from unknown individuals did not warrant further investigation, the sources said. The field office team that reviewed the reported harassing calls determined they did not meet the threshold required for an FBI investigation, and no nexus to terrorism was identified, the sources said. This decision did not sit well with bureau leadership, and the two senior field office agents were removed from their positions, according to the sources. Since taking office last year, FBI director Kash Patel — a fierce loyalist of President Donald Trump — has fired, demoted, or forced into retirement countless career employees who handled past investigations into Trump and his allies. Many of those forced out have filed lawsuits seeking reinstatement. In a statement on an official FBI “Rapid Response” social media account established to tout the agency and respond to critics, Darren Cox, the senior executive who oversees the bureau’s DC office, confirmed the ousting of Burgwald and Rae, but denied the order came from Patel. “This was a personnel decision made at the Washington field office level alone based on our constant evaluation of mission needs,” Cox said. “Any suggestion otherwise is false.” CNN is attempting to locate contact information for Burgwald and Rae. The decision to remove them from their positions has riled many rank and file FBI employees who have been critical of personnel moves they view as highly politicized, sources said. Burgwald graduated from the United States Military Academy West Point and was the recipient of FBI investigative awards, while Rae similarly rose through the ranks of the organization after a lengthy career in national security, sources said. The reassignment of the two senior officials was first reported by Bloomberg Law. In a statement to Bloomberg Law, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Stephen and Katie Miller had no interaction with Burgwald or Rae, adding, “Senior leadership at the FBI determined they were stifling investigations into very serious threats and made a unilateral decision to remove them.” When contacted by CNN, the White House issued the same statement, attributing it to a senior White House official. Still, there is a history of the Millers expressing their displeasure at the FBI’s handling of personal incidents they viewed as threatening in nature. According to people familiar with an incident last year, the couple grew irate with FBI officials over pushback by career agents to use bureau resources to investigate paper flyers critical of Stephen Miller that were posted in the family’s neighborhood. Like several senior Trump officials, the couple later moved into military housing. CNN’s Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/26/politics/fbi-agents-katie-miller-stephen-miller

item.title: 5 arrested near air base used by U.S. in Iran war on suspicion of terrorism
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
LONDON (AP) — U.K. police said that five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks. London’s Metropolitan Police, which takes the lead on potential terrorist activities, said police received a call at 12:45 a.m. related to the three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that is operated by the U.S. under an agreement dating back to the Cold War. The base is home to US bombers striking Iran The arrests come at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states to the U.K., with Russia and Iran among those that have used proxies to commit crimes on their behalf on British soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states including Iran increased 50% in the six months to December 2025. Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iranian missile sites under an agreement with former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who voiced opposition to the war after it was launched by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28. Authorities are investigating a link between the Fairford arrests and Iran as one possibility. Iran has previously indicated that a base used to attack its territory is a legitimate target . U.S. President Donald Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests. “It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great,” he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. “We had them under view for a long time and we got them.” Police feared an explosion The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act in the Whelford area, which backs onto RAF Fairford, which hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron. Aerial footage from Sky News appeared to show a bomb disposal robot roaming between three white trucks. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered around. The robot appeared to be working toward getting access to the third truck. Police gave no details as to the nationality of those arrested. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be detained for up to 14 days without charge, compared to the 24-hour limit for standard arrests, without an extension application. “We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” said Vicki Evans, the Met’s counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator. Evans said a 400-meter (yard) cordon has been put in place around the three vehicles that raised suspicion while the army conducts examinations. As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place. Some have been taken to a nearby recreation center. The U.S. embassy in London warned Americans to be cautious and mindful of their personal security. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he knew the incident would be “deeply concerning” for many. In a post on social media, Burnham thanked police and the armed forces for their response and said he was grateful to the residents who have been evacuated from their homes “while precautionary checks are carried out.” He urged people “not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.” The defense secretaries of the U.S. and the U.K., Pete Hegseth and Wes Streeting, have also spoken about the incident. British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and sabotage attempts in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue. Local residents evacuated as investigation continues Gloucestershire police said the situation appeared to be “contained” and urged residents to follow official advice while the investigation continues. Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said another resident had reported seeing three “suspicious vans” in the village early on Sunday. “There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate,” he said. ___ Associated Press writers Jill Lawless in Liverpool, England, and Ben Finley in Washington, D.C. contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/police-evacuate-homes-near-us-075249083.html

item.description:

A slow-moving nor'easter continued to batter the Northeast on Sunday, bringing more rain, strong winds and another round of coastal flooding after a weekend that killed at least one person. A New York City Housing Authority employee, Leighton Brown, 56, died Saturday afternoon after a tree fell on him in East New York, Brooklyn, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said .
